title: Does Alcohol Help a Cold? The Hot Toddy Myth, Explained
excerpt: Does alcohol help a cold? Why a hot toddy feels soothing, why whiskey doesn't kill germs, how alcohol affects sleep and hydration when you're sick, and the cold medicines you shouldn't mix with a drink.
metaDescription: Does alcohol help a cold? Why hot toddies feel soothing, why whiskey won't kill germs, and which cold medicines you should never mix with a drink.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no, alcohol doesn't help a cold. It doesn't kill the virus, it doesn't shorten the illness, and it tends to work against the things that actually help you recover, like sleep and staying hydrated. The reason the idea sticks around is the hot toddy. A warm mug of tea, honey, and lemon really can make a sore throat and a stuffy nose feel better for a while. The whiskey is the one part of that drink that isn't doing you any favors. If you want the comfort, keep the warm water, honey, and lemon and leave the shot out.

**The quick rules:** One small drink while you have a mild cold is unlikely to hurt a healthy adult, but it won't help either. Don't drink at all if you're taking cold or flu medicine, especially nighttime formulas, because many contain acetaminophen (hard on the liver with alcohol) and sedating antihistamines (dangerously drowsy with alcohol). Skip alcohol if you have a fever, are struggling to keep fluids down, or are short on sleep. Drink water, rest, and give yourself a few days.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and common guidance. It isn't a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** your symptoms last longer than about 10 days, they get better and then suddenly get worse, you have a high fever or a fever that lasts more than a few days, you have a severe sore throat with fever and no cough, or you have ear pain, sinus pain, or wheezing. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you have trouble breathing, chest pain or pressure, confusion, bluish lips, or signs of severe dehydration such as not peeing for many hours. If you've mixed alcohol with cold medicine and someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or vomiting while drowsy, call 911 or Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## Does Alcohol Help a Cold? What the Evidence Actually Says

A cold is a viral infection of your nose and throat. Rhinoviruses cause most of them, though many other viruses, including some coronaviruses, can do it too. There's no cure. Your immune system clears the infection on its own, usually within 7 to 10 days, and everything you do in the meantime is about feeling less miserable and not getting in your immune system's way.

So the real question isn't "does alcohol cure a cold?" (nothing does). It's "does alcohol make the next few days better or worse?" Here's how the pieces line up:

- **Symptom relief:** alcohol has no decongestant, cough-suppressing, or pain-relieving effect that's worth using. The relaxed, warm feeling after a drink is the alcohol acting on your brain and widening blood vessels in your skin. It wears off quickly.
- **Sleep:** a drink may help you fall asleep faster, but alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Rest is one of the few things that genuinely helps you recover, so this is a real cost.
- **Hydration:** alcohol makes your kidneys release more water than they otherwise would. When you're already losing fluid through a runny nose, sweating, and possibly a fever, that's the opposite of what you want.
- **Immune function:** heavy drinking, including a single binge, is known to weaken parts of the immune response. A single small drink is a much smaller deal, but there's no evidence it gives your immune system a boost.
- **Medication safety:** this is the biggest practical risk. Many cold and flu products interact badly with alcohol, and people often don't realize what's in them.

Put together, the most alcohol can do is give you a brief feeling of warmth and relaxation. Everything else is neutral at best and unhelpful at worst.

### What about the studies that say drinkers catch fewer colds?

You may have seen headlines claiming moderate drinkers get fewer colds. These come from a small number of observational studies, the best known being a 1993 study by Sheldon Cohen and colleagues in the *American Journal of Public Health*. They exposed volunteers to cold viruses and found that, among non-smokers, moderate drinkers were somewhat less likely to develop a cold than non-drinkers. A Spanish study published in the early 2000s reported a similar pattern for wine drinkers.

There are three important limits here. First, these studies looked at catching a cold in the first place, not at treating one you already have. Second, they show an association, not cause and effect. People who drink moderately can differ from non-drinkers in income, stress, health, and many other ways that affect how often they get sick. Third, the benefit, if real, only appeared at moderate levels. Heavier drinking is consistently linked with more infections, not fewer. None of this supports having a drink to treat a cold.

## The Hot Toddy for a Cold: Why It Feels Good

The hot toddy is usually some version of whiskey, hot water, honey, and lemon, sometimes with a cinnamon stick or cloves. It has been a home remedy for a long time, and people swear by it. They're not imagining the relief. It's just that the relief comes from the other ingredients.

**Warm liquid.** Hot drinks can make a stuffy nose feel more open and soothe a scratchy throat. A small study from Cardiff University's Common Cold Centre in 2008 found that a hot drink gave people with colds more relief from runny nose, cough, sneezing, sore throat, and tiredness than the same drink at room temperature. The effect is mostly on how you feel, not on how fast the cold clears, but feeling better counts.

**Steam.** Breathing in the steam from a mug can loosen mucus a little and make your nose feel less blocked for a while.

**Honey.** Honey is one of the better-supported home remedies for cough. Reviews of the research, including a Cochrane review on honey for cough in children, suggest it may ease coughing somewhat and help with sleep, and several medical groups list it as a reasonable option. Honey also coats a sore throat. One firm rule: **never give honey to a baby under 1 year old** because of the risk of infant botulism.

**Lemon.** Lemon adds flavor and a little vitamin C. A mug of hot lemon water won't change the course of a cold, but it makes the drink pleasant and encourages you to keep sipping fluids.

**Whiskey.** The alcohol is what makes it a toddy, and it adds the warm, sleepy feeling. It also adds every downside described in this article. A typical toddy has one standard shot (about 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirit), so it's not a huge dose, but it's not doing anything the other ingredients don't already do better.

### A hot toddy without the alcohol

If you like the ritual, you can keep almost all of it. Heat a mug of water to just below boiling, stir in a spoonful of honey, squeeze in half a lemon, and add a cinnamon stick, a few cloves, or a slice of fresh ginger if you have them. Let it steep for a few minutes and drink it slowly, breathing in the steam. Decaf black tea, chamomile, or ginger tea also make a good base. You get the warmth, the throat coating, the steam, and the fluids, and you sleep better than you would with the whiskey.

### Is one hot toddy harmful?

For a healthy adult with a mild cold who isn't taking any medicine, one toddy in the evening is unlikely to cause harm. It just won't help you get better. The problems come from having a few of them, drinking one on top of cold medicine, drinking one when you have a fever or are dehydrated, or using it to knock yourself out so you can sleep. If you decide to have one, make it the only drink of the night, have a full glass of water with it, and don't combine it with any medicine until you've checked the label.

## Whiskey for a Sore Throat: Does Alcohol Kill Germs?

A common version of the myth is that a shot of whiskey or a gargle with spirits "kills the germs" in your throat. It doesn't, for a few reasons.

To reliably kill germs on a surface, alcohol needs to be strong, which is why hand sanitizers are generally recommended at 60% alcohol or higher. Whiskey is about 40% alcohol, and it's diluted further by saliva the moment it hits your mouth. Even more important, cold viruses aren't sitting on the surface of your throat waiting to be wiped away. They've already gotten inside the cells lining your nose and throat, where a swallow of alcohol can't reach them. Your immune system has to clear those infected cells.

Strong alcohol can also irritate the lining of your throat, which is already inflamed. That sting can feel like it's "working," but irritation isn't healing. And swallowed alcohol doesn't stay in your throat; it ends up in your bloodstream like any other drink.

Things that do help a sore throat:

- **Salt water gargles.** About half a teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water, gargled and spat out a few times a day, can ease soreness.
- **Warm drinks with honey,** as above, for adults and children over 1.
- **Lozenges or hard candy** to keep your throat moist (not for small children because of choking risk).
- **Over-the-counter pain relievers** such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, used as the label directs and not combined with alcohol. See our guides to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) for why that last part matters.
- **Humid air.** A cool-mist humidifier or a steamy bathroom can make breathing more comfortable.

A very sore throat with fever, swollen glands, white patches on the tonsils, and no cough can be strep throat, which is bacterial and does need a doctor and possibly antibiotics. Alcohol won't treat that either.

## Can You Drink Alcohol With a Cold?

You can, in the sense that a small amount isn't dangerous for most healthy adults with a mild cold who aren't taking medicine. Whether you should is a different question. Here's what alcohol actually does to the things your body is working on while you're sick.

### Alcohol dehydrates you when you need fluids most

Alcohol blocks a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it around, you pee more than you drink. When you're healthy, that's part of why you wake up thirsty after a night out. When you have a cold, you're already losing fluid through mucus, sweating, and sometimes fever, and you may not feel like eating or drinking much. Dehydration can thicken mucus, make a headache worse, and leave you feeling more drained.

If you do have a drink, match it with at least one glass of water, and keep drinking fluids through the rest of the day.

### Alcohol makes your sleep worse

Sleep is one of the few things that helps when you're sick. Alcohol is a sedative, so it can make you drowsy and help you nod off. But as your body processes it over the night, sleep tends to become lighter and more broken, especially in the second half. Alcohol also reduces REM sleep early in the night. On top of that, alcohol relaxes the muscles of your throat and can worsen snoring and congestion-related breathing problems, which a blocked nose already makes worse.

The result is that a nightcap can mean you fall asleep faster and wake up less rested. If you've noticed this before, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on in more detail.

### Heavy drinking weakens your immune response

Research summarized by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) shows that heavy drinking interferes with several parts of the immune system, from the cells that line your airways to the white blood cells that fight infection. Even a single episode of binge drinking can temporarily dampen some immune responses. Long-term heavy drinking is linked with a higher risk of pneumonia and other respiratory infections.

A single small drink isn't the same as a binge, and there's no good evidence that one drink measurably slows recovery from a cold. But there's also no evidence that it helps, and the more you drink, the more the balance tips against you. Our longer article on [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) covers this research in depth.

### Alcohol can make you feel worse the next day

A cold and a hangover share a lot of symptoms: headache, fatigue, sore muscles, poor sleep, and feeling generally unwell. Stack them and you can feel much worse than either alone, and it becomes harder to tell whether you're getting sicker or just hungover. That matters if you're trying to decide whether to see a doctor.

### Alcohol widens blood vessels in your nose

Alcohol relaxes and widens blood vessels, which is why some people get a flushed face after a drink. The same effect in the lining of the nose can make congestion worse for some people. Some people also find that certain drinks, particularly wine and beer, make their nose stuffier even when they're healthy.

## Cold Medicine and Alcohol: The Real Danger

This is the part of the topic that genuinely matters for safety. Many people treat a cold with an over-the-counter combination product and then have a drink without checking what's in the medicine. Here are the ingredients to look out for on the label.

**Acetaminophen (paracetamol).** It's in Tylenol and in a long list of multi-symptom cold and flu products, including many daytime and nighttime formulas. Your liver processes both alcohol and acetaminophen, and regular heavy drinking makes acetaminophen more likely to damage the liver. The bigger everyday risk is doubling up: taking a cold medicine that contains acetaminophen plus separate Tylenol for a headache, without realizing you're taking the same drug twice. The FDA requires an alcohol warning on acetaminophen products, telling people who have 3 or more drinks a day to ask a doctor before use.

**Sedating antihistamines.** Doxylamine (in many nighttime cold products and some sleep aids), diphenhydramine (Benadryl), and chlorpheniramine all cause drowsiness. Alcohol is also a sedative. Together they can cause much stronger drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and slowed reactions than either alone. Labels on these products warn against drinking alcohol. Never drive after combining them.

**Dextromethorphan.** This cough suppressant is in many cold and cough products. At normal doses it's generally safe, but combined with alcohol it can increase dizziness and drowsiness.

**Decongestants.** Pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine can raise heart rate and blood pressure and make some people jittery. Alcohol can also raise heart rate. The combination isn't usually dangerous for healthy people at normal doses, but it can make you feel shaky and wired, and it can worsen sleep.

**NSAIDs.** Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate the stomach lining, and so does alcohol. Labels warn that people who have 3 or more drinks a day face a higher risk of stomach bleeding.

**Alcohol inside the medicine.** Some liquid cold and cough medicines contain alcohol as an ingredient, which is easy to overlook. Alcohol-free versions are widely available if you'd rather avoid it.

We have detailed guides for the two most common products: [NyQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) and [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol). The short version for both is to wait until the medicine has worn off before drinking, and not to drink while you're actively dosing.

If you're not sure whether your cold medicine is safe with a drink, a pharmacist can tell you in about thirty seconds. That's a much better plan than guessing.

**Antibiotics aren't for colds.** Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics don't work on viruses. If a doctor does prescribe antibiotics for a bacterial infection like strep throat or a sinus infection, ask whether alcohol is a problem with that specific drug. Some antibiotics have well-known alcohol interactions and many don't, but drinking can make it harder to recover either way.

## Does Alcohol Help a Cough or Help You Sleep With a Cold?

People sometimes reach for a nightcap because a cough or blocked nose is keeping them awake. It's an understandable instinct, but it backfires more often than not.

Alcohol might quiet you down enough to fall asleep, but it doesn't suppress the cough reflex in any useful way, and the broken sleep later in the night can leave you more tired than before. Alcohol also tends to worsen acid reflux, which can trigger coughing when you lie down.

Better options for a cough that's keeping you up:

- A spoonful of honey before bed (for anyone over 1 year old).
- Sleeping with your head raised on an extra pillow.
- A warm shower or steam before bed to loosen mucus.
- Saline nasal spray or rinses for a blocked nose.
- A cough or cold medicine chosen with a pharmacist, taken as directed, with no alcohol.

## Does Alcohol Help With the Flu or a Fever?

No, and the reasons are stronger than with a cold. Flu usually hits harder, with fever, body aches, and exhaustion, and it carries a real risk of complications such as pneumonia, especially for older adults, pregnant people, and people with chronic health conditions.

With a fever, you lose more fluid through sweating, so alcohol's dehydrating effect matters more. Alcohol can also make you feel flushed and warm while actually helping your body lose heat through your skin, which muddies how you feel. Many flu remedies contain acetaminophen or ibuprofen, so the medication interactions above apply. And because a hangover can mimic flu symptoms, drinking makes it harder to judge whether you're improving.

If you think you have flu or COVID-19, rest, fluids, and testing are the priorities. Antiviral treatments for flu and COVID-19 work best when started early, so call a doctor quickly if you're in a higher-risk group. Skip the alcohol until you're well.

## What Actually Helps a Cold

Since there's no cure, the goal is to feel more comfortable and give your body what it needs to clear the virus. These are the steps that most medical sources agree on:

1. **Rest.** Sleep as much as you can. Take a day off if you're able, which also keeps you from spreading it.
2. **Fluids.** Water, broth, herbal tea, diluted juice, or an electrolyte drink. Warm drinks are especially soothing. If you're struggling to keep fluids in, our comparison of [electrolyte drinks](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) covers the options.
3. **Honey** for cough and sore throat (not for babies under 1).
4. **Salt water gargles** for a sore throat.
5. **Saline nasal spray or rinses** for congestion. If you use a rinse bottle or neti pot, use distilled, sterile, or previously boiled and cooled water, never straight tap water.
6. **Humid air** from a humidifier or steamy bathroom.
7. **Over-the-counter medicines** for specific symptoms, chosen carefully and taken as directed. Pick single-ingredient products when you can so you know exactly what you're taking, and don't stack products with the same active ingredient.
8. **Eat when you can.** Soup is a classic for good reason: it's warm, hydrating, salty, and easy to eat.

Things with mixed or weak evidence include vitamin C (regular use may slightly shorten colds for some people but taking it once you're sick doesn't seem to do much), zinc lozenges started very early (some studies show a modest benefit, and they can cause a bad taste or nausea), and echinacea (results are inconsistent). Talk to a pharmacist if you want to try any of these, especially if you take other medicines.

## If You Do Decide to Drink With a Cold

Sometimes a cold lines up with a wedding, a holiday dinner, or a work event, and you want to have a drink. If you're a healthy adult with a mild cold, no fever, and no medicine in your system, here's how to keep the downside small:

- **Keep it to one or two drinks** and space them out.
- **Check every medicine you've taken that day.** If any contains acetaminophen, a sedating antihistamine, or dextromethorphan, skip the alcohol or wait until it has worn off. Ask a pharmacist if you're not sure how long that takes.
- **Have a glass of water with each drink,** and drink more water before bed.
- **Eat a proper meal first.**
- **Choose something lower in alcohol** if you can, and avoid high-proof shots.
- **Get to bed at a reasonable hour.** Sleep matters more than usual right now.
- **Don't drive** if you've taken any cold medicine at all with a drink.
- **Stay home if you're very contagious.** In the first few days, when you're sneezing and coughing a lot, you're most likely to pass it on.

And if you have a fever, feel really unwell, or are taking nighttime cold medicine, the right answer is simply to skip it this time.

## When to See a Doctor

Most colds get better on their own within a week to ten days, though a lingering cough can last longer. Call a doctor or visit urgent care if:

- Your symptoms last more than about 10 days without improving.
- You start to get better and then get worse again, especially with a new fever. This can be a sign of a secondary bacterial infection like sinusitis or pneumonia.
- You have a fever above 101.3°F (38.5°C) that lasts more than a few days, or any high fever with a stiff neck, rash, or severe headache.
- You have a severe sore throat with fever, swollen glands, or white patches, especially without a cough.
- You have ear pain, severe sinus pain or pressure, or wheezing.
- You have asthma, COPD, heart disease, diabetes, a weakened immune system, or you're pregnant, and your symptoms are getting worse.

**Get emergency help right away (call 911 in the US) if:**

- You have trouble breathing or are short of breath at rest.
- You have chest pain or pressure.
- Your lips or face look bluish or gray.
- You're confused, very hard to wake, or can't stay awake.
- You have signs of serious dehydration, such as not peeing for many hours, extreme thirst, or dizziness when standing.

**If alcohol has been mixed with cold medicine,** watch for unusual sleepiness, slow or shallow breathing, vomiting while drowsy, or confusion. Those are reasons to call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) right away, rather than letting the person "sleep it off." If you think you or someone else may have taken too much acetaminophen, call Poison Control even if they feel fine, because early treatment matters.

## A Note on DHM and Hangover Supplements

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that some people take around drinking because of research on how it affects alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol. Most of that research is in animals, with limited human data. It's a hangover-support supplement, not a cold remedy. There's no good evidence that DHM helps you fight a cold, shortens an illness, or makes it safe to combine alcohol with cold medicine.

If you're healthy, not taking cold medicine, and planning a night out after you've recovered, some readers use a DHM product such as [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) or [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) alongside the basics of water, food, and pacing. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people typically use it. If you take any regular medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding a supplement.

While you're sick, the better plan is simpler: rest, fluids, honey, and a warm mug of something without whiskey in it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol help a cold?**

No. Alcohol doesn't kill cold viruses or shorten a cold. It can dehydrate you, disrupt your sleep, and interact with common cold medicines. Any relief from a hot toddy comes from the warm liquid, steam, honey, and lemon, not the whiskey.

**Does a hot toddy help a cold?**

The warm liquid, steam, and honey in a hot toddy can make a sore throat and stuffy nose feel better for a while, and honey has some evidence for easing cough. The whiskey adds nothing useful. A toddy made without alcohol gives you the same comfort without the downsides.

**Does whiskey kill germs in your throat?**

No. Whiskey is about 40% alcohol and gets diluted by saliva immediately, while germ-killing sanitizers are generally recommended at 60% alcohol or higher. Cold viruses are also inside the cells lining your throat, where a drink can't reach them. Strong alcohol may irritate an already sore throat.

**Can I drink alcohol with a cold?**

A small amount is unlikely to harm a healthy adult with a mild cold who isn't taking medicine, but it won't help. Skip alcohol if you have a fever, are dehydrated, are taking cold or flu medicine, or are short on sleep. If you do drink, keep it to one or two and have water with each.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking cold medicine?**

It's best not to. Many cold medicines contain acetaminophen, which adds to the strain alcohol puts on your liver, and nighttime formulas often contain sedating antihistamines that become much more sedating with alcohol. Check the label for alcohol warnings and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Does alcohol make a cold last longer?**

There's no good evidence that a single small drink makes a cold last longer. Heavy drinking, though, weakens parts of the immune system and worsens sleep and hydration, all of which can make recovery slower and harder. The more you drink, the more likely it is to work against you.
